issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, in proceedings under Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can direct a person to furnish an interim bond under Section 117(3) only after commencing the inquiry under Section 117(1) and finding a prima facie case.

facts: The case involves proceedings initiated against a person under Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) for the prevention of a breach of the peace.
The central issue is the interpretation of the Magistrate's power under Section 117(3) of the CrPC to demand an interim bond for keeping the peace pending the main inquiry.

The Court considered two conflicting views from various High Courts: one view holding that a bond can be demanded only after the inquiry begins and a prima facie case is established, and another view that it can be done as soon as the person appears in court.
law: Section 117(1) of the CrPC requires that once a person appears before the Magistrate, the Magistrate must "proceed to inquire into the truth of the information upon which the action has been taken."

Section 117(3) of the CrPC allows the Magistrate, "pending the completion of the inquiry under sub-section (1)", to direct the person to execute an interim bond if immediate measures are necessary, and to detain them in custody if they fail to do so.
application: The Supreme Court adopted a strict construction of the Magistrate's powers, emphasizing that the liberty of a person is involved.
The Court reasoned that Section 117(1) and (2) create a mandatory duty for the Magistrate to begin an inquiry into the truth of the information.
The power to ask for an interim bond under Section 117(3) is linked to this inquiry. The phrase "pending the completion of the inquiry" implies that the inquiry must have already commenced.
The Court held that it is not permissible for a Magistrate to simply adjourn the case upon the person's appearance and demand an interim bond without first entering upon the inquiry.

To justify demanding an interim bond, the Magistrate must first begin the inquiry under Section 117(1) and, after considering the matter, be prima facie satisfied about the truth of the information. This prevents the Magistrate's action from being purely administrative and ensures it is based on a preliminary judicial finding.
The Court concluded that if the law were otherwise, a bond could always be insisted upon before the inquiry even began, which is not the intent or wording of the sections.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Magistrate can direct a person to furnish an interim bond under Section 117(3) of the CrPC only after commencing the inquiry as required by Section 117(1) and making a preliminary finding that there is a prima facie case against the person.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 117(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which empowers a Magistrate to demand an interim bond for keeping the peace pending inquiry, is an unconstitutional violation of the fundamental rights under Article 19 of the Constitution.

facts: The case challenged the constitutionality of Section 117(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
This section grants a Magistrate the power to demand an interim bond from a person to keep the peace or maintain good behavior while an inquiry against them (under Section 117(1)) is still pending.
If the person fails to execute the bond, the Magistrate can order their detention until the bond is executed or the inquiry is concluded.
law: Section 117(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows a Magistrate, for reasons recorded in writing, to demand an interim bond if they consider immediate measures necessary to prevent a breach of the peace or disturbance of public tranquility.

Article 19 of the Constitution guarantees fundamental rights, but these rights are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interests of public order, as permitted under clauses (2), (3), (4), and (5) of Article 19.
application: The Court determined that the power under Section 117(3) is intended for emergent situations where there is an immediate danger of a breach of the peace.
It is a preventive measure, not a punitive one, designed to ensure public safety while the formal inquiry into the truth of the information against the person is completed.

The Court rejected the argument that the power could be abused by a Magistrate who might unnecessarily delay the inquiry to prolong detention. It held that the validity of a law is not judged by the potential for its abuse. Furthermore, the law itself (in Section 117(1)) requires the Magistrate to conduct the inquiry expeditiously, and any abuse of this power would be illegal and could lead to the proceedings being quashed.

The Court drew a parallel between this power and the power to detain an undertrial prisoner accused of a cognizable offense. In both scenarios, a person is detained based on a preliminary, ex-parte opinion of a Magistrate to prevent further offenses and ensure the legal process is not defeated.

The Court reasoned that requiring a bond pending a swift inquiry is a necessary and reasonable restriction on personal liberty, especially when a competent authority has formed an opinion that immediate measures are required to maintain peace.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that Section 117(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a valid and reasonable restriction on the fundamental rights under Article 19 of the Constitution and is therefore not unconstitutional.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, in proceedings under Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can direct a person to furnish an interim bond under Section 117(3) only after commencing the inquiry under Section 117(1) and finding a prima facie case.
appellant_arguments: A Magistrate cannot mechanically ask for an interim bond without making any effort to inquire into the truth of the allegations. The inquiry must commence and the Magistrate must find sufficient material to establish a prima facie case before demanding an interim bond.
respondent_arguments: Requiring a full inquiry into the initial allegations before demanding an interim bond would completely defeat the preventive purpose of Section 117(3), which is designed to maintain peace during the pendency of the main proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 117(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which empowers a Magistrate to demand an interim bond for keeping the peace pending inquiry, is an unconstitutional violation of the fundamental rights under Article 19 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The power given to a Magistrate under Section 117(3) to demand an interim bond imposes an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 19 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The provisions of Section 117(3), when properly understood and applied, are reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order and do not offend the fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a), (b), (c), and (d).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The burden of proof to establish that a pre-constitutional law has become void rests upon the party who challenges its validity. The 'preferred-position' doctrine, which presumes the unconstitutionality of a law restricting fundamental rights and places the burden on the state, is not recognized. The expression 'in the interest of public order' is to be interpreted broadly, encompassing not only acts that disturb the security of the State but also those that disturb public tranquility or constitute breaches of the peace.
obiter: The preferred-position doctrine does not have the support of the Supreme Court of the United States.
No one Fundamental Right is superior to another, and Article 19 does not contain a hierarchy of rights.
Vague expressions such as 'the most cherished rights' or 'the inviolable freedoms' sometimes occur in judicial language.
The power to prevent breaches of peace was used in England for over 400 years and is not something needed only for the administration of colonial empires.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The preventive provisions of Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, including Section 117(3), are constitutionally valid as they impose reasonable restrictions on the fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 19. These measures are conceived in the interest of public order, a concept which is broad and elastic enough to include the prevention of crimes, breaches of peace, and disturbances of public tranquility, all of which are necessary for maintaining the even tempo of community life.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the restrictions imposed by the law are 'in the interest of public order' as permitted by Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The court interpreted the expression 'in the interest of public order' as being wider than 'maintenance of public order', and capable of including not only acts which disturb the security of the State but also acts which disturb public tranquility or are breaches of the peace.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the power to demand an interim bond is an unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights under Article 19 was rejected because the court found the provisions to be permissible restrictions enacted 'in the interest of public order'.

The court adopted a broad interpretation of 'public order', holding that it is an elastic expression that encompasses the prevention of breaches of peace and disturbances of public tranquility, thereby bringing the challenged law within the ambit of constitutionally permitted restrictions.
The court found that the limits of the restrictions imposed by the law are well within the scope of clauses (2), (3), (4), and (5) of Article 19, thus negating the claim of unconstitutionality.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the provisions are reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order was accepted by the court.

The court agreed that the prevention of crimes, breaches of peace, and disturbance of public tranquility are directed to the maintenance of the even tempo of community life, and therefore, laws aimed at such prevention are undoubtedly in the interest of public order.

The court affirmed that the expression 'in the interest of public order' is very wide, justifying the preventive measures in the statute and concluding that they do not offend the provisions of Article 19(1)(a), (b), (c), and (d).
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the societal need for preventive measures, stating that 'If prevention of crimes, and breaches of peace and disturbance of public tranquillity are directed to the maintenance of the even tempo of community life, there can be no doubt that they are in the interest of public order.'

The court highlighted the historical and continuing necessity of such powers, noting that the power 'was used in England for over 400 years and is not something which is needed only for administration of colonial empires. Its need in our society today is as great as It was before the British left.'

The court acknowledged the practical reality that occasions may arise where it is not possible to distinguish between peaceful citizens and those whose conduct must be controlled, thus justifying general preventive orders in the interest of public order.
